claims.text: The initial TiVNbTa material is a single-phase BCC dendritic alloy.
TiVNbTa has a yield strength of approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
TiVNbTa has a compressive strength of approximately 423 MPa at 1273 K.
The approximately 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 1273 K are associated with approximately 40% strain.
Adding approximately 0.5–1 at% carbon during TiVNbTa consolidation will form finely dispersed nanoscale carbide precipitates.
Adding approximately 0.5–1 at% carbon may instead or additionally enhance interstitial solid-solution strengthening in TiVNbTa.
Carbon atoms occupying interstitial sites hinder dislocation motion at elevated temperature.
Nanoscale carbide precipitates pin dislocations at elevated temperature.
Carbon-induced dislocation impediment will increase the high-temperature yield strength of TiVNbTa.
Carbon strengthening can increase yield strength without compromising ductility.
Carbon strengthening can increase yield strength without compromising the thermal conductivity needed for W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer.
The carbon-modified alloy will reach at least 450 MPa yield strength at 1273 K.
The carbon-modified alloy will maintain around 40% elongation at 1273 K.
The carbon-modified alloy will preserve sufficient thermal conductivity for effective heat transfer between W and CuCrZr.
Large or coarse carbide precipitates could degrade ductility.
Large or coarse carbide precipitates could degrade thermal performance.

contradictions.description: The baseline strengths are described as occurring with approximately 40% strain, while testing and validation are bounded at up to 30% strain; the predicted outcome nevertheless calls for maintaining around 40% elongation. Strain at measurement, maximum imposed strain, and elongation-to-failure are not consistently distinguished.

The prediction requires at least 450 MPa, an increase of about 36% over 330 MPa, but the strength-based falsification threshold is only a 30% improvement. A result between approximately 429 and 449 MPa would violate the stated prediction without meeting the stated strength falsification criterion.

The mechanism permits either carbide precipitation or interstitial solid-solution strengthening, yet absence of nanoscale carbide features is listed as a falsifying result. Carbide absence would not falsify the alternative interstitial-strengthening branch.
